newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU reasserts right to vet Boeing/McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: EU reasserts right to vet Boeing/McDonnell merger.

text.p: A senior European competition official insisted on Thursday that the EU had the right to review and, if necessary block, the merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas, but he hoped the worst could be avoided.
European competition director Jonathan Faull rejected the companies' view that the EU should let the U.S. authorities take the lead and accept its conclusions.

This view is based on so-called 'positive comity principles' between the European Union and the United States under which anticompetitive practices are normally investigated by the better placed authority -- usually the one where the practices take place.

Using these provisions, the U.S. Justice Department referred to the Commission last month a complaint from airline computer reservation system SABRE, controlled by AMR, about problems accessing a similar system in Europe.

Boeing's vice president for European affairs, Jim Frank, told Reuters on Wednesday that under the positive comity agreement the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) should take the lead role and whatever it decides should be acceptable for the Commission.

But Faull said positive comity did not apply to merger reviews, which in the EU are governed by tight and strict deadlines, but rather to cases where, for example, a company complains it is having problems selling in another country's territory.
"We cannot suspend a merger review while waiting as somebody else looks into it," Faull said.
Faull, who is specifically in charge of international aspects of competition, was replying to questions after a conference at the Centre for European Policy Studies, a Brussels think-tank.

He agreed that the two competition authorities must talk to each other within the limits of confidentiality and ought to avoid a conflict. But the Commission was responsible for the "welfare" of European customers and if the merger was found to be harmful it "may have to say no", Faull said.

He hoped the situation would not get that far, let alone that the Commission would have to levy fines which could be up to 10 percent of the companies' turnover -- which is what would happen if it said 'no' and they went ahead regardless.
"We don't expect this (fines) to happen", he said.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has clearly said he would not allow the merger in its present form and identified Boeing's exclusive long-term supply deals with AMR's American Airlines and Delta Air Lines as posing a particular problem.

The FTC has refrained from comment on the case. But the merger, which is understood to have the backing of the U.S. Defence Department, has won the support of a group of U.S. senators who wrote to President Bill Clinton last week to ask him to ensure the EU review was not "prejudiced".
